name: MCA major territory
summary: The middle cerebral artery major territory is the largest arterial domain of the hemisphere, the lateral convexity from the frontal pole to the occipital pole together with the insula, the temporal lobe convexity and, through the lenticulostriate arteries, the striatum and the internal capsule. This level-2 territory map merges the frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital and insular MCA subterritories with the lenticulostriate domains, and it is the region infarcted by an M1 occlusion: the malignant MCA infarct that swells to threaten herniation and the stroke that carries the whole textbook of hemispheric signs, contralateral face-arm-leg hemiplegia, hemianesthesia, hemianopia, gaze deviation and aphasia or neglect.

anatomy.location: Lateral surface of the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes, the lateral occipital lobe, the insula and opercula, the claustrum and the extreme capsule, and the deep structures supplied by the lenticulostriates (putamen, caudate body, lateral pallidum, upper internal capsule), bounded by the ACA territory along the superior margin, the PCA territory on the inferomedial temporal and occipital surface, and the anterior choroidal territory in the posterior limb.

afferents.from: Middle cerebral artery M1-M4 segments and lenticulostriate arteries

efferents.to: Superficial and deep middle cerebral veins

function: It contains the primary motor and sensory cortex for the face and arm, the frontal eye field, the language areas of the dominant hemisphere and the attention network of the non-dominant one, the auditory cortex, the insula and the striatum, so that occlusion of the stem produces the most extensive single-artery syndrome in neurology. Perfusion depends on the circle of Willis and on leptomeningeal collaterals from the ACA and PCA, which define the penumbra that thrombectomy tries to save; the deep lenticulostriate territory has no collaterals and infarcts first. Complete territory infarction swells over three days and can herniate, especially in young patients with no room for edema.

bestView.label: MCA major territory on the lateral hemisphere
MCA territory from the convexity to the striatum

imaging.normalAppearance: On the territory overlay the MCA domain covers the lateral convexity and the deep striatocapsular region; on CT and MRI the normal territory is the lateral cortex and the lentiform nucleus, with the insular ribbon as its most vulnerable early marker.

pathology.finding: Loss of the insular ribbon and lentiform nucleus, hyperdense M1 sign, then hypodensity of more than two-thirds of the territory with swelling and midline shift by 48-72 hours.
pathology.timing: Decompressive craniectomy within 48 hours improves survival in patients under 60

pathology.finding: Cut-off of the M1 segment with a small core on CT perfusion or DWI and a large penumbra; thrombectomy up to 24 hours in selected patients.
Comma-shaped restricted diffusion of the lentiform nucleus and capsule from lenticulostriate occlusion with M1 recanalization.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Infarction of the motor and sensory cortex and the internal capsule

lesionEffects.deficit: Global aphasia (dominant) or profound neglect and anosognosia (non-dominant)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Infarction of the whole perisylvian language or attention network

lesionEffects.deficit: Gaze deviation toward the lesion and contralateral hemianopia
lesionEffects.mechanism: Frontal eye field and optic radiation infarction
Cytotoxic edema of the whole territory

examination: NIH stroke scale with attention to gaze, fields, language and neglect
Serial level of consciousness and pupils for 72 hours
pearls: The insular ribbon is the first part of the MCA territory to lose its gray-white distinction on CT
A young patient with a whole-territory MCA infarct needs a craniectomy decision before day two
The lenticulostriate part of the territory has no collaterals: it is the core of every MCA stroke
